title: Risks of Racing: Russian and Chinese Perceptions of Strategic Competition in the Euro-Atlantic Region
gist: A CSIS Project on Nuclear Issues study of four U.S. and UK nuclear buildup scenarios concludes Russia and China will not abandon nuclear modernization regardless of Western restraint, because domestic drivers and distrust of the United States dominate; the actionable nuance is that specific capabilities are perceived as far more escalatory than others.

insights.claim: Whether U.S. and allied nuclear investment triggers an arms race depends less on Western force levels than on how Moscow and Beijing interpret those investments.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense-budget forecasts keyed to a mechanical action-reaction arms-race model will misprice the path; watch adversary rhetoric and perception, not just Western procurement lines.
insights.quote: The likelihood of an arms race, however, depends on perceptions in Moscow and Beijing.
insights.locator: As the United States and its allies invest

insights.claim: Russia and China are unlikely to abandon nuclear modernization and expansion programs regardless of U.S. and UK choices, because domestic factors and long-standing distrust of the United States drive those programs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western restraint will not slow Russian or Chinese buildups, implying a structurally higher long-run floor for global nuclear and strategic-defense spending.
insights.quote: The study found that Russia and China are unlikely to abandon their nuclear modernization and expansion programs due to domestic factors and long-standing distrust of the United States.

insights.claim: Russia and China treat certain classes of Western nuclear capability as substantially more escalatory than others, so the composition of a buildup matters more than its aggregate size.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Program-level differentiation matters for defense contractors: escalation risk and political friction cluster in specific capability lines rather than across the whole nuclear portfolio.
insights.quote: Both countries, though, may view investments in certain capabilities as more escalatory than others.

insights.claim: Deterrence and risk-reduction policy should be tailored to Russian and Chinese threat perceptions rather than applied uniformly across the nuclear enterprise.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals a policy direction where arms-control engagement is segmented by capability, keeping some modernization lines politically insulated while others become bargaining chips.
insights.quote: Accordingly, the United States and its allies should tailor deterrence and risk reduction efforts to Russian and Chinese threat perceptions.

insights.claim: The assessment rests on historical sources and expert workshops evaluating four discrete U.S. and UK buildup scenarios, and was funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
insights.speaker: CSIS
entities: UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
insights.so_what: Scenario-based rather than empirical work and UK government sponsorship set the confidence bounds and the likely policy audience for these conclusions.
insights.quote: The CSIS Project on Nuclear Issues (PONI) drew from historical sources and expert workshops to evaluate how Russia and China would view and respond to four U.S. and UK buildup scenarios.
